narrative:
The model predicts you have a 12% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, the school has decided this risk is enough to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is the reason you chose this school—reputation. Unlike many students who passed and focused on the course itself, your choice based on the school's reputation pushed the model toward expecting you might not succeed. The second most important factor is that you have had no past class failures, which is actually the same as the average for students who passed and therefore worked against the failing prediction. However, this positive element was not strong enough to outweigh the other influences. The third key factor is the quality of your family relationships, which you described as good. This also nudged the outcome slightly toward passing, but again could not overcome the dominant effect of your school-choice motivation.

To improve, you should reflect on whether your current study habits truly match the demands of the final year. Even though you want to pursue higher education and study 2 to 5 hours weekly, increasing focused study time, reducing your 10 absences (more than double the average of students who passed), and making sure your motivation is tied to the course content rather than reputation could make a real difference. Taking the remedial courses seriously is a good first step toward strengthening these areas.
